I've just checked it out, on a skeleton file with several sorries that the previous version had already been able to fill in. The new version is very nice, with a globally cleaner code!

I understand that the primary goal is to close the sorries. But getting a clean output is also nice, so you could have a cleaning postprocessing phase (or teaching the language model to do the clean up) doing things like:

  • the model always uses simp +decide [...], but very often the +decide is not necessary, so it could check that and remove it if not needed
  • There are often proofs like := by exact .... Very often, the by exact can be removed in this case, so the model could check if it's the case.

(Not sure if you need to add a phase, or retrain, or just adjust prompts, because I have absolutely no idea how it works behind the scene)

Congratulations, I've been testing Aristotle for quite some time now. For me the biggest difference between this new version and older ones is how much more LLM side have to say through comments. It's good when I'm in exploratory mode and want to get additional arguments, it's bad when I simply want to formalize a note/paper I already have completed and don't want to go over additional stuff. Maybe you could add some kind of configuration for it? Or should I do it more specifically just through prompts?

It's really cool to see you have now git like structure with multiple .lean files. I guess what's missing but will be an obvious step for you is actually being able to connect projects on Aristotle with Github repositories and being able to push it there. This can be done through Terminal, but would be great to have on webUI as well.

BTW, I have tested the new Aristotle Agent on Erdos Problem 488 and it's working very nicely. Here's the formalization by Aristotle of this blueprint note by GPT-5.4. In this case, I had a longer discussion with GPT-5.4 and then a loop Aristotle-GPT-5.4.

I wanted to ask about the new version of the agent (haven't tested yet): is Lean currently invoked on my machine, or Harmonic's servers? (to provide feedback to the agent). The CLI I tested a while ago could only send a problem to Harmonic, and wait until it does something with it.

If it is just on my side, then the version-pinning & available Mathlib would not be necessary, I suppose (but helpful) -- that is is how standard coding agents work. Or does it have to be on Harmonic servers because it is doing very extensive search?

@Przemek Chojecki @Sébastien Gouëzel thanks for the feedback, I agree on both of these stylistic points and we will work on them over the next few days, and hopefully have some improvements out shortly!
One advantage of this new release is that many of these behaviours can be controlled via appropriate prompting from the user to adjust to their taste, but we do want the out of the box experience to be as good as possible so that users don't need very long prompts to get a good result.

For tighter GitHub integration, I agree and we've heard that from other users too so will definitely be seeing what we can do there.

@Mirek Olšák all lean interaction / proof search etc takes place on Harmonic's servers still.

I've tried a prompt to improve the result to conform more to Mathlib, as follows:

I would like you to cleanup the file ..., as follows:

  • If a proof is := by exact ..., try to see if you can eliminate the by exact and still get a working proof
  • If a simp call includes +decide but works without it, then remove it
  • If a command generalize_proofs can be removed, remove it.
  • If a Mathlib linter fires, try to understand the issue and fix it
  • Remove the character ; when not needed
  • No space after ⟨ and no space before ⟩
  • When counting characters, really count characters and not unicode code points.
  • If a line is less than 100 characters, never split it.
  • If a line is more than 101 characters, then split it at reasonable points. If possible, you should avoid too short lines after the split: minimize the number of resulting lines.

It works well for many things, but not for line splitting: they are split way too short (more around 60 characters than 100) and I couldn't figure out a good prompt for that.

I've also tried this version and I confirm it is much more efficient. It now really looks like a working tool rather than an extremely well-crafted gadget, and this makes a huge difference. I believe that GitHub integration would be great, and even better the opportunity of customizing the output: this e-mail thing works, but it is sometimes a bit unpractical. Ideally, I would like to be able to launch Aristotle from the CLI and either set a local folder or a github repo; in the latter case, it might open a PR to the repo rather than producing new files; in the former, it could send an e-mail when it is done, leaving the user decide whether they want to receive the whole tar or to pick just one/two files from the online server..

This file states the 15 inequalities from the Lemma in Section 3 of the paper.

I had the same "Complete with errors" message on a project where I didn't provide a toolchain or any files other than a pdf (since the docs say this is supported). In this case, does that mean the project had trouble reading the pdf?

More precisely, in general, COMPLETE_WITH_ERRORS means that the agent does not believe it successfully completed the task it was asked to perform.

In some cases, this reflects an actual issue with the user-provided input or uploaded files (PDF are in fact supported). In other cases, it simply means the agent behaved unexpectedly in that particular run, and the user can often just resume and try again.

I haven't received it myself, but "complete with errors" seems to be a particularly confusing error message, since the run did not "complete" or "finish" in any useful sense. Could it be changed? What about "could not complete task"? That might at least induce some users to simply try again.

I've been experimenting a bit with the new version of Aristotle and although I find it very nice, there is one thing that I consider a regression. What happens is a ChatGPT-like behaviour of always telling me that I'm right even if I'm wrong, resulting in a discrepancy between my requests and the formalised results. In particular, I tried with the following three prompts:

  1. Prove that there are only finitely many imaginary quadratic fields
  2. Prove that in a profinite group the commutator subgroup is closed, hence the abelianisation is automatically compact
  3. Prove that L^p([0,1]) is reflexive

Each of the three above results is false: what Aristotle did, in each case, was to turn it to the "closest" (to its taste) right(-ish) result, and formalise that one. In details,

  1. It said "I formalized and proved that there are only finitely many imaginary quadratic fields whose ring ℤ√d is a principal ideal domain, in the file RequestProject/ImaginaryQuadratic.lean" which is somewhat ok-ish (the ring ℤ√d is not the ring of integers in half of the cases, so the fact that it is not principal does not imply that the "field is principal", a statement which does not in principle make any sense but is typically understood as meaning that the ring of integers is). So, it turned my stupid question about the existence of finitely many imaginary fields, which is clearly false, into a mathematically interesting one, and then once more tried to translate the statement into something accessible, although wrong.
  2. It said something along the lines of "in the context of profinite groups, one normally considers the abelianization in the category of compact groups, hence I proved commutator_topologicalClosure_isClosed: The topological closure of the commutator subgroup is closed.: which is tautological, hence not very interesting. It also commented about a result saying that when the group is topologically finitely generated, the commutator is indeed automatically closed by a very deep result of Nikolov–Segal (2007). Of course, it could not provide a proof of the latter.
  3. Was turned into proving that L^p([0,1]) is reflexive for p<∞p<\inftyp<∞, with some discussion about the case 1<p≤21<p\le 21<p≤2 and nothing about the case 0≤p<10\le p<10≤p<1 (where the claim is false).

I find all this a regression; it gives the feeling of something "cool", but as a mathematician who does not have a clue, say, about LpL^pLp-spaces, I would like an answer "what you wrote is false, here a counterexample". If we move forward and statements become more and more intricate, I think it is important that the tool avoid allucinations on statements: the fact that the proofs are correct, since Lean-checked, is nice of course: but it is short of being really useful. If I'm prompting something about a single theorem, I can check the statement in detail (and provided I'm sufficiently expert in Lean), in order to compare it with what I actually wrote informally; but if I launch Aristotle on a full project and I need to check that all theorems have not been changed, I will jus waste a lot of time. The previous version was much less ambitious: it was also much weaker in Lean proofs, and that was a pity, but at least it stuck to informal statements much more.
